bp: An e-commerce platform wants to rank marketing campaigns for users, but the training signal it needs is not directly written in the data. The site may know that a user saw a campaign and later bought something, yet the campaign itself may say something like a seasonal theme, a lifestyle promise, or a creative slogan rather than naming exact products. The sales log records concrete purchases, while the campaign text speaks in broad intent. This paper serves the system that must connect those two worlds before it can learn which campaigns are worth showing. The ordinary object is a campaign whose meaning has to be translated into product types in the platform taxonomy. Once that translation exists, purchases in those product types can become positive labels for ranking models. Campaign-2-PT-RAG is therefore not mainly a ranking model; it is a way to manufacture consistent supervision for campaign ranking when direct influence labels are scarce.
wh: The difficulty is that campaign influence is hidden behind two layers of ambiguity. First, marketing language is intentionally indirect. A campaign may suggest an activity, a mood, or a collection without naming every product type it is meant to promote. Simple product matching misses this implicit intent. Second, purchase logs do not say why a user bought an item. A user might buy a product after seeing a campaign because the campaign mattered, or because they already planned to buy it. The abstract focuses on the first layer: without product-level attribution, supervised learning for campaign optimization remains limited. The system needs labels at large scale, but expert annotation of campaign-to-product-type mappings is expensive and does not naturally cover every new campaign. The tension is between scale and trust: labels must be generated automatically, yet they must be close enough to expert mappings that downstream rankers do not learn from noisy coincidences.
naive: A smart beginner might search each campaign for product names and label any later purchase of those products as campaign-driven. That fails because campaign copy often uses thematic language rather than product vocabulary. Another beginner might ask a language model to directly list final product types and accept the answer. That is risky because a broad language guess can be too loose, hallucinate product categories, or ignore the platform's actual taxonomy. A third option is to treat any purchase after exposure as positive, but that confuses timing with influence. The paper's problem exists because none of these shortcuts gives large, consistent labels tied to what the campaign actually promotes.
ap: The core idea is to turn a vague attribution problem into a controlled semantic alignment task. Instead of asking, "Did this campaign cause this exact purchase?" the system first asks, "Which product types does this campaign appear to promote?" It uses a large language model to read the campaign content for implicit intent, then retrieves candidate product types from the platform taxonomy using semantic search, which means looking for product categories whose meanings are close to the interpreted campaign meaning rather than merely sharing the same words. A structured language-model classifier then judges each candidate product type for relevance. The accepted product types form a campaign-specific coverage set. User purchases that match this set become positive training labels for later campaign ranking models. This gives the ranker a usable target while keeping the label generation anchored to the platform's known product taxonomy.
mech: The mechanism starts with campaign content and a product taxonomy. The campaign content is the creative text or description whose product meaning is not explicit. The taxonomy is the platform's organized list of product types, such as the categories under which purchases are recorded. First, a language model interprets the campaign content. In plain terms, it reads past slogans and surface words to infer the product intent that a human merchandiser might recognize. Second, the system uses that interpreted meaning to retrieve candidate product types from the taxonomy. This retrieval step narrows the search space: instead of judging every possible product type, it gathers a smaller set whose descriptions or meanings appear close to the campaign. Third, a structured language-model classifier evaluates each candidate. Structured matters because the classifier is not merely free-writing; it is asked to make a relevance decision for each product type. The candidates that pass become the campaign's product coverage set. Fourth, the platform compares user purchase records against that coverage set. If a user bought a product whose type is covered by the campaign, that event can be turned into a positive label for downstream campaign ranking. The output is not the final ranked campaign list. It is a label table that ranking models can train on: campaign, user or purchase context, and a positive signal derived from semantic product-type attribution.
math: The main mathematical ideas are similarity search, classification, and supervised ranking labels. Similarity search begins with the problem of choosing which differences matter. Campaign wording and product taxonomy entries are not identical strings, so the system needs a way to place meanings close when they refer to related product intent. In everyday terms, it asks which product types sit near the campaign's inferred meaning, while accepting that compressing meaning into a closeness score can lose nuance. Classification then turns each candidate into a relevance decision: belongs in the campaign coverage set or does not. That is a boundary-drawing problem under uncertainty, because the abstract says the language model evaluates each product type's relevance rather than reading a ground-truth answer from the data. The final mathematical move is supervised learning for ranking. A ranker needs examples of what should count as a successful campaign-user match. The generated purchase labels supply those examples, so later training can adjust scores toward campaigns associated with matched product-type purchases. The tradeoff is coverage versus precision: a wide coverage set catches more influenced purchases but risks false positives, while a narrow set is cleaner but may miss campaign intent.
dots: This paper connects to ranking because its labels are built for downstream campaign ranking optimization: the eventual system must sort campaigns by expected usefulness for users or business goals. It connects to retrieval because the product taxonomy is too large to inspect naively, so the method first pulls a candidate set by semantic closeness. It connects to language-model work because the hard information is implicit human intent in campaign copy, not a clean numeric feature. It also sits near recommendation and advertising papers that struggle with missing feedback: platforms often observe clicks, purchases, and exposures, but not the hidden reason a user acted. Compared with ordinary product recommendation, the object being matched is indirect. The campaign points to a family of products, the user buys a concrete item, and the system has to bridge that middle layer before learning can begin. The recurring conference idea is turning messy behavioral evidence into usable training supervision.
ww: The approach should work better than keyword matching because it preserves the kind of meaning marketers actually use. A campaign can imply product types through occasion, style, audience, or theme; a language model can interpret those signals more flexibly than a literal word list. It should also work better than unconstrained generation because retrieval keeps the model tied to the platform taxonomy. The classifier judges candidates that already exist as product types, so the output is easier to compare with expert-annotated campaign-product-type mappings. Once the coverage set is formed, purchase matching becomes mechanically simple: if the purchased product's type is inside the campaign's inferred coverage, the event can contribute a positive label. The deeper reason is that the method inserts an interpretable middle object between campaign text and purchase labels. Product type is coarse enough to absorb creative language but concrete enough to match transactions. That middle object reduces ambiguity before the ranking model sees the data.
po: The payoff is scalable label generation for campaign ranking in production e-commerce environments. The abstract reports validation on internal and synthetic datasets against expert-annotated campaign-to-product-type mappings, with the supplied text stating 78 to 90 percent precision. That means the automatically produced mappings are often close to expert judgments, at least under the reported evaluation. Practically, the platform gets a repeatable way to create positive training labels without hand-labeling every campaign, allowing downstream ranking models to learn from campaign influence signals that were previously too ambiguous to use at scale.
limits: The method assumes the campaign content contains enough interpretable signal to infer product intent. It also assumes the product taxonomy is accurate, sufficiently detailed, and described in a way that semantic search can retrieve the right candidates. The purchase-derived positives are still indirect labels: matching a campaign's product type does not prove the campaign caused the purchase. The abstract reports precision against expert mappings, but the supplied text is truncated after "precis," so recall, downstream ranking gains, and failure cases are not fully visible here. The approach may also miss campaigns whose intent is deliberately broad, mixed, or dependent on images and layout not represented in the input text.
